steps.title: What you see: revenue is too high
steps.plain: The shop sold four orders worth ₹2,790, but the dashboard says ₹4,770. The event stream delivers 'at least once': event e3 arrived twice (a retry 6 seconds later), and order 1003 also has a second event when it changed from placed to paid. A pipeline that copies bronze straight to silver counts order 1003 three times.
steps.code:
-- the pipeline as written
CREATE TABLE silver AS SELECT order_id, amount, status, _ingested_at FROM bronze

steps.title: Naive fix: add DISTINCT
steps.plain: DISTINCT removes rows that are identical in every column. But the two copies of e3 were ingested at different times, and the paid update has a different status: none of them are identical. Revenue is still ₹4,770. Worse, every query downstream now needs its own DISTINCT, and each will be wrong in its own way.
steps.code:
-- the naive fix, added to the dashboard query
SELECT DISTINCT order_id, amount, status, _ingested_at FROM dupes.silver

steps.title: Right fix: latest row per key, then MERGE
steps.plain: Silver keeps one row per business key (order_id): the most recent event, by ingestion time. MERGE on order_id writes it, so a retried batch, a duplicate event or a re-run changes nothing. Ran the MERGE twice on purpose: still 4 rows and ₹2,790. Order 1003 shows its latest status, paid.
steps.code:
w = Window.partitionBy('order_id').orderBy(desc('_ingested_at'), desc('event_id'))
latest = bronze.withColumn('_rn', row_number().over(w)).filter('_rn = 1')

MERGE INTO dupes.silver_ok t USING latest s ON t.order_id = s.order_id
WHEN MATCHED AND s._ingested_at > t._ingested_at THEN UPDATE SET *
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
-- run twice: same result

steps.title: Right fix: replace exactly the day you load
steps.plain: The job takes the date as a parameter and atomically replaces only that day's partition (replaceWhere). Run it once or ten times: the result is the same, and the other 26 days are never touched. Look at the last commit: it removes and adds only the 27 October files. Never read 'today' from the clock inside a job; pass the date in, so the same job can backfill any day.

steps.title: What you see: history that cannot be true
steps.plain: Today's batch for customer history has three traps: two changes for Asha (C-77) in one batch (Mumbai on 1 Nov, Sydney on 15 Nov), a 'change' for Ravi (C-80) that changes nothing, and a late, older change for Asha (Goa on 20 Oct) that arrived last. One MERGE for the whole batch fails outright: [DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE] Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched and attempted to modify the same. Looping row by row in arrival order 'works', but now Asha's current city is Goa (it should be Sydney), 1 version(s) end before they start, and Ravi has 2 versions of the same city.

steps.title: Right fix: rebuild the history of affected keys, in source order
steps.plain: For every customer touched by the batch, take all of their changes ever (old and new), order them by when they happened in the source (changed_at, never load time), drop changes that change nothing (hash equals the previous one), and derive valid_to from the next version. Then replace just those customers' rows in one atomic write (replaceWhere). Ran twice. Asha: Pune → Goa (20 Oct) → Mumbai → Sydney, current = Sydney; on 25 Oct she lived in Goa. Ravi: still one version.
steps.code:
WITH affected AS (SELECT DISTINCT customer_id FROM batch),
     ordered AS (
       SELECT c.*, sha2(concat_ws('|', city, email), 256) AS h,
              lag(sha2(concat_ws('|', city, email), 256)) OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) AS prev_h
       FROM scd.changes c JOIN affected USING (customer_id)),
     versions AS (SELECT * FROM ordered WHERE prev_h IS NULL OR h <> prev_h)      -- drop no-op changes
SELECT customer_id, city, email, changed_at AS valid_from,
       lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) AS valid_to,
       lead(changed_at) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY changed_at) IS NULL AS is_current
FROM versions

# replace only the affected customers, atomically
hist.write.format('delta').mode('overwrite').option('replaceWhere', "customer_id IN ('C-77','C-80')").saveAsTable('scd.silver')

steps.plain: Grouping by the batch (arrival day) instead of the event date makes the totals add up overall, but it puts order 2005 on 27 Oct. 27 Oct would show ₹1,919, 26 Oct still ₹750. Both days are wrong now, and they disagree with the source system's own reports.

steps.title: Right fix: rebuild exactly the days the batch touched
steps.plain: Ask the batch which event dates it contains (2026-10-26, 2026-10-27), and rebuild exactly those days' partitions, by event date. Late data lands on the day it happened, and only the touched days are rewritten (see the last commit). For streams, the same idea is a watermark: how late data may be and still count.

steps.title: Naive fix: just run the whole job again
steps.plain: Re-running from the top inserts the batch into silver a second time (4 rows now), and gold sums it: revenue ₹2,400 instead of ₹1,200. A failure turned into a duplicate.

steps.title: Right fix: every step safe to repeat, plus a run log
steps.plain: Each step is idempotent (MERGE into silver, replace the day in gold) and records itself in a run log. After the crash, the re-run skips silver (already done) and builds gold. Ran it twice more: silver 2 rows, revenue ₹1,200. And a crash inside a single Delta write is harmless: a write failed on a bad row mid-way, the table stayed at version 1 (was 1), and readers still see 2 rows. Half a write is never visible; at worst it leaves orphan files that VACUUM removes.
steps.code:
def job(batch):
    if not run_log.done('silver', batch):
        MERGE INTO silver USING batch ON order_id ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
        run_log.mark('silver', batch)
    replace_day(gold, '2026-10-27')            # overwrite one partition
    run_log.mark('gold', batch)

job('b-1')  # 💥 after silver
job('b-1')  # resumes: skips silver, builds gold
job('b-1')  # again: changes nothing
